title: Wells and hospitals
hookLine: the edicts list shade trees, wells, and medicine for people and animals (Rock Edict 2)

cards: Midday on a dusty road. A trader leading an ox, a mother with a child on her hip, a stray dog with its tongue out, all looking for the same two things: water and shade.
You might expect a royal inscription to list palaces and victories. Ashoka's second rock edict lists something smaller and stranger: medicine, herbs, wells, trees along the road.
And it says, more than once, that these are for people and for animals alike.

teach.b: First, care for two kinds of patient. Rock Edict Two says the king arranged medical care for people and for animals; translators give treatment, or care.
Whether there were hospital buildings, the stone doesn't say, and it's honest to leave it there. Second, herbs where there were none.
Where healing plants, roots and fruits didn't grow, they were brought in and planted, and not only in his own lands: the edict says this reached neighboring kingdoms too. Third, the road.

teach.h: WELLS AND TREES ON THE ROADS.
teach.b: Wells were dug and trees planted along the roads, for people and animals. A pillar inscription fills in the picture: banyans for shade, mango groves, wells, rest houses, places for animals to drink.
Who benefits from a shade tree? Not the king, and usually not the person who plants it. Whoever walks by, years from now, on a hot afternoon.
Fourth, why a Buddhist king would care. The Vinaya, the monastic rulebook, tells of a monk lying sick in his own filth, with no one tending him. The Buddha and Ananda wash him and lay him down.
Then the Buddha tells the monks, in effect: you have no mother and father here; if you don't care for one another, who will?
Whoever would tend the Buddha, he says, should tend the sick. The edict doesn't mention that story, but they share an instinct: care that doesn't ask who deserves it, even for the dog on the road.

how: Buddhist teachers hold up Ashoka's public works as an example of generosity in practice, and the Vinaya story of the sick monk makes tending the sick part of monastic life.

games.why: Rock Edict Two lists care for people and animals, healing herbs planted, and wells and trees along the roads.

practice: Picture the places you pass through each day, a street, a hallway, a shared kitchen, and ask what small thing would make one of them easier for a stranger: picking up litter, refilling the water, holding a door.
Choose one that nobody needs to know you did, and hold the picture of it for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Edict. Ashoka's rock inscription listing care for people and animals: herbs planted, wells dug, trees along the roads.
